title: Delhi Police Probe Reveals Extent of Violence During CJP's Parliament March
excerpt: Facial recognition identified nearly 3,000 individuals with criminal records among protesters during the July 20 Sansad Chalo march, as the aftermath sparks a national debate over surveillance, policing, and student rights.
body:
A Student March That Shook Central Delhi

On July 20, 2026, tens of thousands of young Indians marched from Jantar Mantar toward Parliament House in New Delhi in what became the most consequential street protest India has seen in years. Organized by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), the "Sansad Chalo" march was timed to coincide with the opening day of Parliament's Monsoon Session, pressing demands over the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak scandal and calling for the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2083780416872611892

What began as a student-led demonstration spiraled into hours of violent confrontation. By evening, more than 130 security personnel and 65 protesters had been hospitalized, 15–20 police vehicles lay damaged, and 15 FIRs had been registered, some carrying charges as severe as attempt to murder.

How the Violence Unfolded

Delhi Police had imposed prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita Sanhita (BNSS) banning assemblies of five or more people in the New Delhi district and deployed over 5,000 personnel, closing five Delhi Metro stations near Parliament. The CJP had not obtained permission for the march.

Around 11:25 a.m., the marchers reached Parliament Street and attempted to push through barricades. Police responded with lathi charges and tear gas at multiple locations, including Parliament Street, Patel Chowk, and Rail Bhawan. Internet services were suspended in parts of central Delhi.

"When a non-violent protest is taking place, what is the reason for a lathi charge?"

— Shashi Tharoor, Member of Parliament

Officials say the stone pelting was not limited to the initial confrontation near Parliament. Police released CCTV and mobile phone footage showing groups hurling stones at officers near Regal Cinema in Connaught Place's Outer Circle and attempting to vandalize vehicles near Rajiv Chowk — areas well beyond the barricade zone. FIRs were registered at both the Parliament Street and Connaught Place police stations, covering rioting, assault on public servants, obstruction of government duties, and snatching of police gear.

Facial Recognition and the Surveillance Backlash

In the days following the march, Delhi Police deployed AI-enabled Facial Recognition Systems (FRS) through mobile surveillance vehicles to analyze CCTV footage from the protest site. The automated system cross-referenced live footage against criminal databases, identifying 2,873 individuals with prior criminal records — of whom 989 faced serious charges.

The breakdown was striking: 101 individuals linked to murder cases, 62 to attempted murder, 284 to robbery and dacoity, 61 to rape (including POCSO cases), 229 under the Arms Act, and 67 under narcotics laws. Delhi Police cited these numbers to argue that criminal elements had infiltrated the student movement.

But the surveillance has triggered a fierce legal and civil liberties backlash. The Internet Freedom Foundation wrote to Delhi's police commissioner demanding deletion of biometric data collected at the protest site. A CPI(M) MP moved the Supreme Court challenging the constitutionality of mass facial recognition at peaceful protests. A separate PIL in the Delhi High Court is listed for hearing on September 11.

"We need proportionality even if we are to claim national security risks. Accountability must flow both ways."

— Akash Karmakar, technology law partner, Panag & Babu

Reuters reported that police officers were also seen noting the Instagram handles of protesters arriving at the site — a practice one inspector justified as screening for criminal backgrounds.

Political Fallout and Resolution

The march's political impact was immediate. Under mounting pressure, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned five days later, and the CJP subsequently called off its 36-day protest at Jantar Mantar. CJP spokespersons had earlier met Union Minister J.P. Nadda on the margins of the protest, raising demands for activist Sonam Wangchuk's release, Pradhan's resignation, and ₹1 crore compensation for families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide.

The Delhi government announced that no legal action would be taken against student protesters, though proceedings would continue against individuals with criminal records. Four state governments — Assam, Bihar, Maharashtra, and Delhi — have announced withdrawal of cases against students.

The police response drew condemnation from opposition leaders including Rahul Gandhi and Arvind Kejriwal, and from cultural figures spanning Bollywood and the music industry — among them Arijit Singh, Shabana Azmi, Alia Bhatt, and filmmaker Anurag Kashyap. Allegations of plainclothes officers without badges participating in the crackdown, and the use of pellet guns that left an Outlook journalist and a 19-year-old protester with eye injuries, have added fuel to demands for an independent inquiry.

What It Means for the Indian Diaspora

For Indians abroad, the Sansad Chalo march has become a flashpoint in ongoing conversations about democratic freedoms and state surveillance in India. The use of facial recognition technology against protesters — in the absence of any governing legislation — raises questions familiar to diaspora communities already navigating debates over digital privacy and civil liberties in their adopted countries. The NEET paper leak scandal, which drove the protests, directly affects families with children preparing for India's hyper-competitive medical entrance exams, many of whom invest years and lakhs in coaching from abroad.

What's Next

The Supreme Court petition challenging facial recognition surveillance and the Delhi High Court PIL on police conduct, set for September 11, will be closely watched. With Pradhan's resignation partially satisfying protester demands, the focus now shifts to whether systemic reforms in examination integrity follow — and whether the precedent of mass biometric surveillance at protests becomes normalized or is checked by the judiciary.
